PARIS, France (CNN) -- Opposition lawmakers on Tuesday derided President Nicolas Sarkozy for returning France to NATO's military command after an absence of more than four decades, yet they proved unable to halt the measure when it was put to a vote. French troops now patrol alongside the Afghan army as part of the NATO mission in Afghanistan.

The National Assembly endorsed Sarkozy's plan by a margin of 329 to 238. Socialist Laurent Fabius, a former prime minister, addressed Prime Minister Francois Fillon directly: "You tell us this would mean more independence and more influence. It would probably mean less independence and less influence."

Although the move did not technically require parliamentary approval, the president's party deliberately scheduled the debate to afford opponents an opportunity to voice their views -- and to demonstrate that a majority stood behind the initiative. Submitting the issue to a vote in the National Assembly also underscored just how sensitive the matter remains in France.

France was a founding member of the NATO alliance in 1949, but it withdrew from the military structure in 1966 amid mounting friction with the United States. "To cooperate is to lose your independence," French President Charles de Gaulle declared at the time.

For the following 43 years, even as France selectively participated in NATO military operations, de Gaulle's principle endured as the governing cornerstone of French foreign policy. The reasoning held that if Paris were to take orders from NATO military commanders, the nation would forfeit complete control over its own destiny.

Sarkozy, however, holds the opposite conviction -- namely, that cooperation within NATO serves as a guarantee of French independence. Rejoining NATO's military command, he contended, would secure France a seat at the table for critical decision-making.

From its earliest years, the organization's trans-Atlantic ties were strained, as U.S. analysts cautioned that should the European allies fail to increase their contributions to the alliance, they risked losing the support of the United States, according to NATO. The European nations, for their part, felt that the United States was seeking to dominate the organization, NATO noted.

De Gaulle's 1966 decision meant that no French forces could serve under permanent allied command and that France would take no part in defense planning. In 1995, France rejoined NATO's military committee, which advises the alliance's political authorities on military policy and strategy and provides guidance on military matters to NATO's strategic commanders. Even while remaining outside the military command, France contributed both troops and funding to NATO activities, including operations in Kosovo and Afghanistan. Indeed, half of all French troops stationed abroad are assigned to NATO military operations.

Opponents of Sarkozy's move -- among them several members of his own party -- maintain that de Gaulle, not Sarkozy, had it right. They launched a last-minute petition drive in an effort to halt his return to NATO. "With this decision, France will return as a subordinate country and will lose its ability to represent another image in the world," said Nicolas Dupont-Aignan, a member of the French National Assembly.

The president's allies, by contrast, calculate that Sarkozy's move will strengthen Europe's hand on defense issues. "There will be more European weight in the way decisions will be made," said Louis Giscard d'Estaing, a member of the National Assembly's U.S. Friendship Committee. "Therefore, the balance of power between the USA and Europe will be re-established within this French move."

CNN's Sunaina Karkarey and Jim Bittermann contributed to this report.

As part of the ongoing NATO mission, French soldiers currently patrol Afghanistan alongside that country's army.

By a margin of 329 to 238, the National Assembly approved Sarkozy's proposal. Addressing Prime Minister Francois Fillon, Socialist and former Prime Minister Laurent Fabius remarked: "You claim this will bring us greater independence and greater influence. In all likelihood, it will bring the opposite—diminished independence and diminished influence."

Although parliamentary consent wasn't strictly necessary for the decision, Sarkozy's party arranged the debate to allow critics an opportunity to express their views—and simultaneously to demonstrate that a majority supported the plan. Putting the question before the National Assembly also underscored just how touchy the subject remains within France.

France helped establish the NATO alliance back in 1949, but it withdrew from the military framework in 1966 during a period of tension with the United States. "Cooperation means surrendering your independence," declared French President Charles de Gaulle during that era.

Over the following 43 years, France chose to take part in certain NATO military efforts, yet de Gaulle's doctrine continued to serve as the foundational principle of the country's foreign policy. The logic held that if France were to submit to NATO's military leadership, it would forfeit full command over its own future.

Sarkozy, by contrast, holds the reverse view—maintaining that partnership within NATO actually safeguards French independence. He contended that returning to NATO's military command grants France a place among those who shape decisions.

According to NATO, tensions across the Atlantic emerged early in the organization's history because American experts cautioned that European members risked losing U.S. backing unless they boosted their contributions to the alliance. At the same time, NATO notes, European countries suspected the United States of attempting to control the organization.

Under de Gaulle's 1966 ruling, French military forces could not be placed under permanent allied command, and France would take no role in defense planning. Then in 1995, France rejoined NATO's military committee—the body that counsels NATO's political leadership on strategy and military policy while advising the alliance's strategic commanders on military affairs. Even though France remained outside the military command, it still supplied both personnel and financing for NATO undertakings, such as operations in Kosovo and Afghanistan. Indeed, half of all French forces stationed abroad are committed to NATO military missions.

Those against Sarkozy's decision—among them certain members of his own party—maintain that de Gaulle, rather than Sarkozy, understood the matter correctly. They launched an eleventh-hour petition campaign to halt his return to NATO. "Through this decision, France comes back as a subservient nation and forfeits its capacity to project a different image on the world stage," stated Nicolas Dupont-Aignan, who serves in the French National Assembly.

Sarkozy's supporters, however, reckon that his decision will bolster Europe's influence in defense matters. "European influence over how decisions get made will grow," observed Louis Giscard d'Estaing, who sits on the National Assembly's U.S. Friendship Committee. "As a result, this French initiative will restore equilibrium in the power dynamic between the United States and Europe."

CNN's Sunaina Karkarey and Jim Bittermann contributed to this report.

**PARIS** — France moved to fully reintegrate into NATO's military command structure after decades on the sidelines, as President Nicolas Sarkozy secured a crucial parliamentary victory that reversed one of the defining foreign policy stances of the Fifth Republic.

The National Assembly voted 329 to 238 in favor of the government's position, following a confidence motion tied to the decision. The vote effectively ended more than 40 years of French military independence from the alliance's integrated command, a separation that dated back to President Charles de Gaulle's landmark 1966 decision to withdraw.

## A Reversal of Gaullist Doctrine

De Gaulle pulled France from NATO's integrated military command in 1966, asserting national sovereignty and independence from what he viewed as American dominance of the alliance. While France remained a member of NATO politically and never left the organization entirely, it stood apart from its command structures for decades.

Sarkozy has framed the reintegration as a pragmatic recognition of reality, arguing that France can wield greater influence from within the alliance's decision-making bodies rather than from outside them.

"A solitary nation is a nation that has no influence," Sarkozy argued in defending the move, insisting that full membership would strengthen rather than diminish French sovereignty. His government emphasized that France would retain full independence over its nuclear deterrent and would not be obligated to commit forces to operations it opposed.

## Supporters Cite Influence and Modernization

Backers of the decision, largely from Sarkozy's governing majority, argued that France's partial separation had become an outdated relic of Cold War politics. They contended that with French troops already participating in NATO operations, including in Afghanistan, remaining outside the command structure denied France a seat at the table where key military decisions were made.

Supporters also pointed to the move as complementary to efforts to build a stronger European defense capability, arguing that a France fully engaged in NATO would be better positioned to advance European security interests.

## Opponents Warn of Lost Independence

The decision drew sharp criticism across the political spectrum. Socialist opposition figures accused Sarkozy of surrendering a cornerstone of French foreign policy and aligning the country too closely with the United States.

Critics warned that reintegration would compromise the independent voice France had cultivated on the world stage, a voice notably exercised when France opposed the 2003 U.S.-led invasion of Iraq.

Some members within Sarkozy's own broader political family, including those who consider themselves heirs to the Gaullist tradition, expressed unease about abandoning a principle established by the founder of their movement.

Former Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin was among the prominent voices who questioned the wisdom of the reversal, reflecting divisions that reached beyond the traditional left-right divide.

## What Comes Next

With parliamentary backing secured, France was positioned to take up command positions within NATO's structure and participate fully in its military planning bodies. The government maintained that key elements of French autonomy would remain untouched, seeking to reassure a skeptical public and political class that the nation's independence was not being sacrificed.

The debate underscored enduring tensions in French politics between Atlanticist engagement and the Gaullist legacy of strategic independence — a tension that Sarkozy's decision brought into sharp relief.

# France's National Assembly Debates Sarkozy's NATO Reintegration Plan

## Historic Decision Reopens Decades-Old Debate on French Military Independence

**PARIS** — France's National Assembly became the stage for an impassioned debate as lawmakers confronted President Nicolas Sarkozy's controversial decision to return the country to NATO's integrated military command structure, ending more than four decades of strategic distance that dated back to General Charles de Gaulle's landmark 1966 withdrawal.

The debate exposed deep divisions over national sovereignty, France's role in the transatlantic alliance, and the legacy of Gaullist foreign policy that has shaped the nation's defense posture for generations.

## The Historical Context: De Gaulle's 1966 Break

To understand the weight of Sarkozy's decision, one must return to 1966, when President de Gaulle withdrew France from NATO's integrated military command—though notably, not from the alliance itself. De Gaulle's decision reflected his vision of French independence and his suspicion of American dominance within the Western alliance.

The General famously ordered all foreign troops off French soil, prompting the relocation of NATO's headquarters from Paris to Brussels. De Gaulle sought to establish France as an independent power with its own nuclear deterrent—the *force de frappe*—capable of pursuing foreign policy free from Washington's influence.

This decision became a cornerstone of French national identity, symbolizing the country's determination to maintain strategic autonomy and its distinctive voice on the world stage.

## Sarkozy's Case for Reintegration

President Sarkozy argued that France's absence from NATO's command structures had become an anachronism that diminished rather than enhanced French influence. Supporters of the reintegration contended that France was already participating substantially in NATO operations while lacking a corresponding voice in the alliance's strategic decision-making.

The government maintained that full reintegration would:

- **Increase French influence** within NATO's command structure and strategic planning
- **Strengthen European defense** by demonstrating France's commitment to collective security
- **Preserve nuclear independence**, as Sarkozy insisted the *force de frappe* would remain under exclusive French control
- **Reflect contemporary realities** in a post-Cold War security environment

Government officials emphasized that France would not compromise its ability to make independent decisions about deploying its own forces.

## Opposition Voices

The proposal drew fierce criticism from across the political spectrum. Socialist and other opposition members argued that the decision represented a betrayal of Gaullist principles and an unnecessary surrender of hard-won independence.

Critics raised several key objections:

- Concerns that reintegration signaled excessive alignment with American foreign policy
- Fears about diminished French strategic autonomy
- Questions about whether France would gain meaningful influence commensurate with its concessions
- Arguments that the decision abandoned a distinctive French tradition without adequate justification

Some Gaullists within Sarkozy's own political camp expressed unease at reversing a policy so closely associated with the founder of their movement.

## The Broader Significance

The debate touched on fundamental questions about France's identity and its place in the world. For decades, the Gaullist stance on NATO had transcended ordinary politics to become a symbol of national pride and independence.

Sarkozy's push for reintegration reflected his broader foreign policy vision, which included warmer relations with the United States and a stronger commitment to building European defense capabilities within the NATO framework.

## Conclusion

The National Assembly debate underscored the enduring power of historical memory in shaping contemporary French politics. As lawmakers weighed the merits of reintegration, they grappled not only with practical questions of defense strategy but with the symbolic weight of departing from a path set by one of France's most revered leaders.

The decision marked a significant moment in French foreign policy, closing a chapter opened by de Gaulle and repositioning France within the Western alliance for a new strategic era.

---

# France and NATO: A Complex Alliance, 1949–2009

In March 2009, President Nicolas Sarkozy announced that France would fully rejoin NATO's integrated military command structure, ending more than four decades of self-imposed distance from the alliance's operational core. The decision was historic, controversial, and deeply symbolic—closing a chapter that had begun with Charles de Gaulle's dramatic break in 1966. To understand the significance of Sarkozy's move, one must trace the long and often turbulent history of France's relationship with the Atlantic Alliance.

## Founding Member, 1949

France was among the twelve founding signatories of the North Atlantic Treaty in April 1949. In the aftermath of World War II, with Western Europe economically shattered and facing the growing power of the Soviet Union, France saw clear value in a collective defense arrangement anchored by the United States. The mutual defense guarantee enshrined in Article 5—an attack on one is an attack on all—offered security against both Soviet expansion and any resurgence of German militarism, a concern that loomed large in French strategic thinking.

In these early years, France was an enthusiastic participant. Paris hosted NATO's headquarters, and French officers played prominent roles in the alliance's command structures. Yet beneath this cooperation, tensions were already forming over questions of national sovereignty, nuclear policy, and American dominance of the alliance.

## Growing Discontent Under de Gaulle

The return of Charles de Gaulle to power in 1958 marked a turning point. De Gaulle harbored deep reservations about an alliance in which, he believed, France occupied a subordinate position to the United States and Britain. His vision of French *grandeur* demanded strategic independence—the ability to make sovereign decisions about war and peace without deferring to Washington.

Several grievances animated de Gaulle's frustration:

- **American dominance:** De Gaulle resented what he saw as an "Anglo-Saxon" duopoly directing alliance affairs. In 1958, he proposed a tripartite directorate that would give France equal say alongside the US and Britain. The proposal was rejected, deepening his disillusionment.

- **Nuclear sovereignty:** France was developing its own independent nuclear deterrent, the *force de frappe*. De Gaulle was unwilling to subordinate French nuclear forces to an American-controlled command, insisting that a nation's ultimate defense could not be entrusted to a foreign power.

- **Loss of control:** The presence of foreign troops and nuclear weapons on French soil, outside French command, was increasingly intolerable to a leader who prized national autonomy.

## The 1966 Break

In 1966, de Gaulle acted decisively. While France remained a member of the North Atlantic Treaty and its political framework, he withdrew French forces from NATO's **integrated military command structure**. This was a crucial distinction: France did not leave the alliance altogether but removed itself from the unified command that coordinated allied military operations.

The consequences were dramatic. De Gaulle ordered all foreign troops off French soil, forcing NATO to relocate its headquarters from Paris to Brussels, where they remain today. American and Canadian bases in France were closed. France retained the political benefits of membership—including the Article 5 guarantee—while reclaiming full sovereign control over its armed forces.

This posture defined France's "exceptionalism" within the alliance for the next forty years. Paris maintained its independent nuclear deterrent and reserved the right to make autonomous military decisions, positioning itself as a distinct voice within the Western camp.

## Cooperation Amid Independence

Despite its formal absence from the command structure, France never truly abandoned the alliance. Throughout the Cold War, French and NATO forces maintained close informal coordination, particularly regarding the defense of West Germany. Secret arrangements ensured that French troops stationed in Germany would cooperate with allied forces in the event of a Soviet attack.

France's semi-detached status was, in practice, more nuanced than its rhetoric suggested. It remained firmly within the Western bloc, sharing the alliance's fundamental commitment to collective defense while preserving symbolic and practical independence.

## Gradual Rapprochement After the Cold War

The end of the Cold War in 1991 transformed the strategic landscape and reduced some of the original rationale for French aloofness. Over the following years, France began a gradual, cautious return toward the alliance's structures.

French forces participated actively in NATO operations in the Balkans during the 1990s, including in Bosnia and Kosovo. In 1995, President Jacques Chirac took steps to bring France closer, rejoining some military committees. However, a full return stalled over French demands—rejected by the United States—that a European officer be given command of NATO's Southern Command in Naples.

By the 2000s, France was participating in the majority of NATO's military bodies and contributing significantly to alliance operations, including in Afghanistan. The gap between France's formal position and its actual involvement had narrowed considerably, making full reintegration seem increasingly logical.

## Sarkozy's Decision, 2009

When Nicolas Sarkozy became president in 2007, he brought a more openly pro-Atlantic and pro-American orientation to the Élysée Palace. He argued that France's partial absence from NATO's command structures diminished its influence rather than enhanced its independence. By sitting outside the rooms where key decisions were made, France was limiting its ability to shape the alliance from within.

At NATO's 60th-anniversary summit in April 2009, Sarkozy formalized France's full return to the integrated military command. He framed the decision not as a surrender of sovereignty but as its opposite—a way to reclaim French influence and secure senior command positions for French officers. Importantly, France retained key elements of its independence: its nuclear deterrent remained under exclusive national control, and Paris reserved the right to decide whether to commit forces to any particular operation.

Sarkozy paired the move with a renewed push for a stronger European defense identity, arguing that a more integrated France within NATO and a more capable Europe were complementary, not contradictory, goals.

## Controversy and Legacy

Sarkozy's decision provoked fierce debate in France. Critics across the political spectrum—including Gaullists who cherished de Gaulle's legacy and figures on the left—warned that reintegration compromised the independent foreign policy that had distinguished France on the world stage. They feared alignment with American strategic priorities and an erosion of the nation's autonomous voice. Sarkozy survived a parliamentary confidence vote on the issue, but the controversy underscored how deeply de Gaulle's vision remained embedded in French political culture.

Supporters countered that the world of 2009 bore little resemblance to that of 1966. With the Soviet threat gone and France already deeply engaged in NATO operations, full membership simply reflected reality while maximizing French influence.

## Conclusion

The arc of France's relationship with NATO—from enthusiastic founder in 1949, to defiant outsider under de Gaulle in 1966, to full reintegration under Sarkozy in 2009—reflects the enduring French tension between alliance solidarity and national independence. De Gaulle's break was a bold assertion of sovereignty at the height of the Cold War; Sarkozy's return was a pragmatic recognition that influence in the twenty-first century required a seat at every table. Yet even in rejoining, France preserved the nuclear independence and decisional autonomy that de Gaulle had fought to secure—suggesting that the Gaullist spirit endured, even as its most visible expression came to an end.
